archetype.name: Dual-Threat (scramble-first)
archetype.definition: A quarterback whose best plays come when the pocket breaks down and he runs for first downs, and whose passing works underneath and over the middle of the field but not deep.

report.headline: A scrambler whose legs outran his passing, now on IR at QB3
report.take:
Malik Willis got the job he spent four years waiting for, and eight starts settled what the Green Bay cameos could not. Those 2024 and 2025 lines (ypa ranked 1st both years, CPOE 1st in 2025) came from two or three games each, mostly managed snaps. As a full-time starter he has been a below-average passer: -0.083 EPA per dropback (38th of 55), CPOE of -5.06 (42nd), and a 1-7 record. The 2025 comparison of a 27-point CPOE drop isn't a collapse. It is a tiny sample regressing to what he looks like with a full workload. The 2022 Titans line (-0.459 EPA per play) was never an outlier.

What drives the season is the gap between his passes and his dropbacks. Every charted depth group on his throws added EPA: short 0-9 (+0.171 a play) and intermediate 10-19 (+0.251) were both genuinely good. His passing EPA still totals -19.3, because sacks, screens and turnovers swallow those gains. Throws behind the line cost -9.6. He takes a sack on 10.3% of dropbacks (44th of 55), and 3 lost fumbles rank 51st. His scrambles hand much of that back. Twenty-four of them averaged +0.709 EPA and produced 12 first downs, which is why his all-dropback total (-4.6) is far less damning than the passing number alone.

The numbers hide how much of the sack problem is his own. Miami's pressure rate is not the issue: the offense's hit rate ranks 18th. His time to throw is 3.06 seconds, and he has had a high pressure-to-sack rate every season of his career (60th of 60 in 2024, 60th of 62 in 2025). He holds the ball looking for something to open up, and that is the same instinct that produces the scrambles. The trade roughly pays off on the ground. It doesn't pay off in the passing game, because the deep ball doesn't reward the extra time: 22.2% completions and 3 interceptions on 20+ yard throws.

Where it heads is out of his hands for now. He is on injured reserve with a core/groin injury, with an expected return of December 13 and surgery not foreseen. Kyle McCord started Weeks 10 and 11, and the depth chart lists Willis third. His last three games were his best passing stretch: +0.05 EPA per dropback and CPOE up 4.4 points on his season. That came against the 29th, 24th and 27th defenses, though, and it ended with a -8.7 passing EPA against Detroit. It is not enough to make him the obvious answer when healthy.

strengths.title: Scrambles that move the chains
strengths.body: His scrambles are the most efficient thing he does: +0.709 EPA each, with half of them converting first downs. The cause is the same patience that hurts him in the pocket. He waits, the coverage turns its back, and he runs. This has held across every stop of his career (his rushing totals rank respectably each year), so it is a lasting trait rather than a hot streak.

strengths.title: Short and intermediate throws work
strengths.body: When he throws on time to the 0-19 yard area, the offense moves: +0.171 EPA on short throws with a 57% success rate, and +0.251 on intermediate throws with a slightly positive CPOE. Caleb Douglas and Greg Dulcich were the main beneficiaries. This is the version of Willis that beat the Jets in Week 7, and it is a real skill. It just isn't enough to carry the whole dropback.

concerns.title: Sacks are a career-long habit
concerns.body: A 10.3% sack rate and 34.3% pressure-to-sack rate are the cost of how he plays. He has ranked at or near the bottom in pressure-to-sack every year he has played, and his time to throw is over three seconds. It is partly the price of the scrambles. But 24 sacks in eight games is the single biggest reason his passing EPA is negative, and it won't go away.

concerns.title: Deep ball and ball security
concerns.body: Throws of 20+ air yards connect 22.2% of the time, with a CPOE of -15.8 and 3 interceptions. Add 3 lost fumbles (51st of 55) and 5 turnover-worthy fumbles. This is a real accuracy and ball-security flaw, not a role artifact. The bad-throw rate jumped to 14.4% from the tiny 2025 sample, and the 2022 starts looked similar.

concerns.title: Packers cameos set false expectations
concerns.body: His 2024 and 2025 seasons ranked near the top in efficiency, but across only three and two games. Eight starts in 2026 put him 38th in EPA per dropback. The full-time sample is the one to believe.

trend.note: Weeks 1-5 were mostly negative passing games, bottoming out at -9.8 against Minnesota's top-ranked defense. The bye-week return brought his best stretch (+10.1 EPA vs the Jets, +3.1 vs New England). Detroit then knocked him back to -8.7 before the injury and the switch to McCord.

nextGame.headline: He's on IR; this is McCord's start, not his
nextGame.body:
Willis will not play Week 12. He is on injured reserve with an expected return of December 13 and sits third on the depth chart. On paper this would have been his kind of game. The Jets' defense ranks 29th in pass EPA allowed and 29th on short throws, the area where he is most efficient. His best start of the year came against them in Week 7. The catch is that the Jets have the 5th-best sack rate, which is exactly the pressure that drags his numbers down.

For Miami, the start belongs to Kyle McCord. The Dolphins are 3.5-point home underdogs with a 40.5 total, and they are without WR Jared Wayne (a 33% snap player). The Jets will be missing DT David Onyemata (46% of snaps), which slightly thins their interior rush. Willis' only stake in this game is whether McCord plays well enough to keep the job once Willis is healthy.

keyMatchups.title: Short-area passing against a soft underneath defense
keyMatchups.body: New York allows the 29th-worst EPA on short passes, which fits the quick-game version of Willis. It also fits McCord, who gets this game. If Willis returns in December, this is the profile of defense where his short and intermediate efficiency plays.

keyMatchups.title: Jets sack rate versus his holding
keyMatchups.body: A top-five sack rate meets a quarterback who holds the ball over three seconds. That collision is why even a weak Jets pass defense is not a clean matchup for him.

keyMatchups.title: The Week 7 blueprint
keyMatchups.body: His win over the Jets came on quick throws (5.1 intended air yards, zero bad throws) plus 37 rushing yards. That game is the template for how he can be efficient. It is also a reminder that it worked against a bottom-five defense.

nextGame.watch: How McCord handles the Jets' pass rush, which decides whether Willis has a job to come back to in December.

restOfSeason.body:
The base case is that Willis returns around mid-December as a backup and starts again only if McCord struggles or Miami wants another look. If he does start, expect the same shape. The rushing should hold up because the scrambling is a career-long trait. The passing will be roughly average per attempt but dragged down by sacks and turnovers. The late-season TD bump (5.1% over his last three) is the piece most likely to fade back toward his 2.9% season rate.

The core and groin injury adds a layer of risk to the part of his game that works. A quarterback recovering from that injury may scramble less, and his value depends on those scrambles. The ranges below assume he starts; if he stays at QB3, his output is zero.
swingFactors: Whether he gets the starting job back from McCord
How the core/groin injury affects his scrambling

confidence.note: He is on IR and listed QB3, his return date is an estimate, and he has only an eight-start sample.
